analytic.title: Enhanced Schedulability Tests for Real-Time Regularity-Based Virtualized Systems with Dependent and Self-Suspension Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: As virtualization becomes increasingly popular, more critical applications that require real-time performance guarantees are deployed on virtualized systems. In such systems, the Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling (HiRTS) framework divides the scheduling problem into task-level scheduling and resource-level scheduling. Specifically, resource-level scheduling divides a physical resource into multiple resource partitions while task-level scheduling schedules the tasks on each resource partition. Accordingly, the Regularity-based Resource Partitioning (RRP) model offers efficient resource-level scheduling. Despite the availability of adequate resource-level tools, the task-level scheduling based on the RRP model still has a scope for improvements. To extend the applicability of the RRP model under a variety of task workload environments, this paper offers:
(1) a more practical schedulability test for independent tasks whose key parameters, i.e., Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), period and deadline, are non-integral multiples of a time slice;

(2) a tuned Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling approach and a corresponding schedulability test for intra-VM dependent tasks; (3) schedulability tests for self-suspended tasks based on Fixed-Relative-Deadline (FRD) scheduling strategies.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Virtualization is becoming increasingly popular since it integrates multiple systems, i.e., Virtual Machines (VM), on the same computing platform. In a virtualized platform, a multitude of cloud-native applications (tasks) require real-time performance guarantees [1]. To host such applications, the CPU resource supply allocated to each VM should ensure realtime performance guarantees. Real-time scheduling of such tasks on VMs and real-time scheduling of VMs on physical resources (CPUs) collectively constitute the specifications of a Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling (HiRTS) framework, as shown in Fig. 1. In general, the framework is divided into two levels i.e., Resource Level and Task Level. The CPU share allocated to a VM is called a resource partition 1 . Tasklevel scheduling ensures that the task set assigned to a VM is schedulable given the information of the resource partition allocated to a VM. Resource-level scheduling ensures that each VM is allocated a desirable resource partition. This paper mainly focuses on task-level scheduling in the HiRTS framework.

Based on the HiRTS framework, different resource partitioning models have been proposed to characterize the resource 1 A formal definition of resource partition is given later in Section II. partition allocated to each VM. Specifically, resource partitioning models such as the Regularity-based Resource Partitioning (RRP) model [2], the Periodic model [3], and the Explicit Deadline Periodic model [4] have been proposed. In this paper, we focus on the RRP model because it is more efficient in resource utilization [5], as explained in Section II.

Although there has been extensive research on the RRP model [2,6,7,8,9], most previous works focus on resourcelevel scheduling. The existing task-level schedulability tests [2,7] only apply to tasks, whose key parameters such as arrival time, Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), deadline, and period, are all integral multiples of the time-slice length. We categorize such tasks as restricted tasks. A new schedulability test that can handle any tasks besides the restricted tasks is urgently required. This paper proposes a new schedulability test for EDF that applies to restricted and non-restricted tasks within a VM, which is scheduled by a RRP resource scheduler.

Several complications can arise when interdependency between tasks is considered. Such inter-dependent tasks deployed inside the same system are practical cases to be considered. In some cases, one task may take the output of another task as an input, resulting in an interdependency between jobs [10,11]. In other cases, jobs may need mutual exclusive access to some shared resources, e.g., data structures and files, which also leads to interdependency [12]. Some studies have been performed on graph-based models that reveal interdependency between tasks [10,11,12]. However, no previous works have been conducted to explore the scheduling of inter-dependent tasks on a VM based on the RRP model. Inspired by [10], this paper introduces a tuned scheduling approach of interdependent tasks within a given VM and also proposes a corresponding schedulability test.

In addition, Inter-Partition Communication (IPC) and various I/O operations are widely used in virtualized systems. For instance, applications deployed on the virtualized systems may need to read values from external devices, such as sensors, or receive messages from other VMs through IPC [13]. Yet no schedulability tests regarding such task sets have been proposed based on the RRP model. By modeling IPC and I/O operations as segmented self-suspensions [14], this paper introduces inter-dependent and I/O aware scheduling and corresponding schedulability tests based on the RRP model.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: In this section, we first introduce the definition of the RRP model, together with the benefits offered by this model compared to other resource partitioning models. Then, we briefly review the previous works on the RRP model and the scheduling of inter-dependent tasks and self-suspended tasks.

div.head: A. The RRP model
div.p: First, we define a time slice as the basic unit of time at the resource level.

Definition 1: Time slice is the basic time unit within which a VM cannot be preempted by another VM. The length of each time slice, referred to as β, is fixed before generating a unique cyclic schedule of VMs following the ARINC 653 cyclic scheduling policy [1] for a given CPU. In the following parts of the paper, timing parameters are represented in time slices, unless otherwise specified. For example, time slice 0 refers to the time interval [0, β). In a virtualized system, each VM is allocated a fraction of a CPU, resulting in a resource partition, which is a set of time slices as defined below [2].

Definition 2: Resource partition A is a tuple (S, p). Time slice sequence S =< s 1 , s 2 , s 3 , ...., s q > where 0 < s 1 < s 2 < s 3 < ... < s q < p and p is the partition period with the following semantics. The CPU is available to the VM owning resource partition A for time slice
div.formula: s k + x • p where x ∈ Z nonneg , 1 ≤ k ≤ q.
div.p: Definition 3: The supply function S(t) of resource partition A is the number of allocated time slices during [0, t). For example, resource partition A r in Fig. 2(a) has A r = (S, p) where p = 7 and S =< 0, 1, 3, 5 >. Accordingly, S(1) = 1, S(2) = S(3) = 2, S(4) = S(5) = 3 and so on. The RRP model [6,9] parameterizes a resource partition by: (1) availability factor, the resource supply rate; (2) supply regularity, the difference between the actual resource supply and the ideal resource supply, which temporally allocates the resources evenly across the schedule.
Definition 4: The availability factor α(A) of a resource partition A is defined as α(A) = q p .

Definition 5: For a resource partition A, instant regularity is defined in terms of supply function and availability factor, i.e., I(A, t) = S(t)t • α(A). Supply regularity R(A) is an integer w that satisfies: |I (A, i) -I(A, j)| < w, ∀i ≥ j.
For instance, the availability factor of A r in Fig. 2(a) is 4/7. The instant regularity is I(A r , 2) = 6/7, I(A r , 7) = 0 and so on. In the schedule for A r , the maximum instant regularity is
div.formula: I(A r , 2) while the minimum is I(A r , 7). Since |I(A r , 7) - I(A r , 2)| < 1, the supply regularity of A r is R(A r ) = 1.
div.p: Definition 6: If the supply regularity of a resource partition A is 1, i.e., R(A) = 1, A is a regular partition. Otherwise, A is an irregular partition.

Unique to the RRP model, the supply regularity reflects the difference between the RRP model and other resource models, e.g., the Periodic model [3] and the Explicit Deadline Periodic (EDP) model [15]. Bounded by the supply regularity, a regular partition approximates the ideal resource supply better in comparison to an irregular partition with the same availability factor. Take the resource partitions in Fig. 2 as an example. Fig. 2(a) shows the schedule of a regular partition with an availability factor of 4/7. The supply function of a regular partition A r at a given time instance t is i.e., s(t), is plotted on the y-axis while time (in the unit of time slice) is the x-axis. The green dotted line indicates the ideal CPU resource supply, i.e., 4/7 of every time slice is allocated to A r . However, this is not possible since a time slice is an indivisible unit of time at the resource level. The solid red line indicates the actual CPU resource allocation to the VM during its period. The RRP model uses the concept of regularity to constantly minimize the difference between the actual and ideal CPU resource allocation to each and every VM that is scheduled. To further strengthen the benefit of regularity, let us consider how the Periodic model schedules this resource partition in Fig. 2(b) as an example. Note that the resource partition in Fig. 2(b) is regarded as an irregular partition by the RRP model. The resource partition A i with the same CPU resource usage as regular partition A r i.e., availability factor of 4/7 ≈ 57.14%, is assigned continuous time slices.

Bounded by the supply regularity, the longest zero-CPU resource supply interval for A r is 1 while that for A i is 3. In addition, assume a sporadic task scheduled on A i arrives at time 4 with Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) as 1 time slice and relative deadline as 2 time slices. This task cannot meet its deadline on A i as no time slices have been allocated to A i during interval [4,6]. On the contrary, this task, when scheduled on A r , will not miss its deadline though both resource partitions (A r , A i ) have the same CPU resource usage. It is also worth noting that irrespective of the change in the arrival time of the sporadic task, the task will not miss its deadline when scheduled on A r . Henceforth, without a formal definition of supply regularity, other resource models such as the Periodic model and the EDP model may generate irregular partitions and thus require a larger CPU resource usage to schedule the same task. div.head: B. Previous works on the RRP model
div.p: As introduced above, the RRP model is more efficient in resource utilization due to the definition of the supply regularity. However, the existence of the supply regularity also makes it NP-hard to schedule a set of resource partitions on a set of CPUs [2]. To generate resource-level schedules in polynomial time, each resource partition will be allocated a larger fraction of the CPU than it requires, leading to a resource utilization overhead. Therefore, most previous works focus on resource-level scheduling based on the RRP model [6,5,16,8,9] trying to minimize the resource utilization overhead or to generate resource-level schedules efficiently under different scenarios, i.e., with online reconfiguration [9] or transient faults [8].

There is hardly any research on task-level scheduling based on the RRP model. With [2] proposing basic task-level schedulability tests for algorithms Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Rate Monotonic (RM) on restricted task sets, [7] further extends the results by proving that all scheduling techniques for single-core scheduling can directly be applied in task-level scheduling of restricted task sets in a VM.

However, the conclusion given in [7] does not work for nonrestricted tasks, let alone inter-dependent or self-suspended tasks. To bridge the voids, this paper discusses the scheduling and schedulability tests of different types of task sets on a VM based on the RRP model, which has not been conducted so far to the best of our knowledge.

div.head: C. Previous works on inter-dependent tasks
div.p: Tasks with interdependency widely exist in many practical systems. Specifically, tasks that rely on other tasks' output and tasks that need mutual exclusive access to some shared resources can all result in interdependency between tasks [10,12]. Such interdependency can always be modeled as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) [10,12,17].

To solve the real-time scheduling problem of interdependent tasks, [10] first proposes a tuned EDF algorithm for uni-processor rendezvous task scheduling. This approach calculates the effective deadline for each job and uses the effective deadline for EDF scheduling. Later on, [17,18] further extends the real-time scheduling of synchronous tasks to multi-core scenarios using partitioned and global EDF. After that, [19] further extends the research to optimize the energy efficiency of the real-time scheduling of DAG tasks.

Despite these efforts, real-time scheduling of DAG tasks on a VM has not been studied to the best of our knowledge. While the idea of previous works remains applicable [10] since each VM takes a part of a CPU, which is similar to single-core scheduling, there is a critical difference between scheduling on a VM and scheduling on a CPU. On a dedicated CPU, a node in the DAG N i whose WCET is c i will be completed when scheduled to execute in c i wall-clock time [20]. However, on a VM, the wall-clock time needed for the VM to retain c i execution time is always longer than c i because the VM only occupies a fraction of the CPU. This key difference results in mandatory modifications in the tuned EDF approach in [10]. Thus, in this paper, we introduce the tuned EDF for intra-VM dependent tasks, examine the optimality of the approach with the modifications applied, and propose a corresponding schedulability test.

div.head: D. Previous works on self-suspended tasks
div.p: A task may self-suspend when it needs to wait for other internal or external activities [21,22]. The real-time schedulability analyses for traditional tasks that do not self-suspend cannot be directly applied to self-suspended tasks without any modifications [21]. To analyze the schedulability of selfsuspended tasks, based on different assumptions of selfsuspensions, the self-suspension models are categorized into segmented, dynamic, and hybrid self-suspension models [22].

The segmented self-suspension model [23] is the most restrictive since it assumes the information of each computation phase and the time of suspension between any computation phases are pre-known. Dynamic self-suspension model [24], on the contrary, assumes no such information is available. The hybrid self-suspension model [25] combines both segmented and dynamic by assuming that the number of suspension intervals is known while the specific execution time in each computation phase stays unavailable. As an initial effort to bring self-suspension models to virtualized systems, we mainly consider the most restrictive model, the segmented self-suspension model, which is applicable to many cases in embedded systems. Therefore, we mainly introduce the state of the art of the segmented self-suspension model.

Based on the segmented self-suspension model, multiple scheduling policies are proposed, including EDF-based and fixed-priority preemptive scheduling algorithms [21]. Based on the scheduling algorithms, corresponding schedulability tests are offered [26]. The speedup factor [14] is used to analyze the performance of different scheduling algorithms and a Fixed-Relative-Deadline (FRD) algorithm performs well with a constant speedup factor [14].

Despite a large number of previous works, the selfsuspended task scheduling has not been explored in virtualized systems yet to the best of our knowledge. In virtualized systems, it is common for tasks to self-suspend. For instance, an embedded virtualized system designed for avionics [13] may need to read data from external devices like sensors and the task must remain self-suspended until the data is retrieved. As an initial effort to bring a self-suspension model to virtualized systems, we employ the segmented self-suspension model and the FRD scheduling algorithm as a part of task-level scheduling based on the RRP model. Then, we present novel schedulability tests for self-suspended task scheduling based on the RRP model.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY TEST FOR UNRESTRICTED INDEPENDENT TASKS
div.p: Based on the RRP model, a task-level schedulability test needs to determine whether a set of tasks on a VM is schedulable on a resource partition allocated to the VM with the knowledge of the availability factor and supply regularity of the resource partition. Thus, the input of a schedulability test should always contain a task set T = {T 1 , T 2 , ..., T n } and a resource partition A's availability factor α(A) as well as supply regularity R(A). Specifically,
div.formula: T i ∈ T has T i = (c i , d i , p i ).
div.p: Here, c i and d i are the WCET and relative deadline of task T i . If T i is a periodic task, p i is the period. If T i is a sporadic task, p i is the minimum separation time interval. As mentioned above, the parameters of each task are represented in time slices. For instance, a task T i 's WCET is 10ms and the timeslice length β = 5ms. The c i is then 2 representing that the WCET of the task is 2 time slices. A task T i is a restricted task if its key parameters, i.e., c i , d i and p i , are all integers.

[7] transforms several real-time scheduling problems on a VM to equivalent problems on a dedicated single CPU. Accordingly, schedulability tests are established for different task-level schedulers based on the RRP model. However, the schedulability tests developed only apply to task sets where all tasks are restricted tasks. In this paper, we focus on the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) because it is the optimal task scheduling algorithm on a single core and on a single resource partition [2]. The same problem exists for other scheduling algorithms as well and it can be solved in a similar fashion as mentioned below. Next, we present a sufficient schedulability test for a restricted periodic task set T to be schedulable on a given resource partition A.

Theorem 1: [2] For a periodic task set T , if for any task T i ∈ T , WCET c i , deadline d i , and period p i are all integers, the sufficient condition for the task set T to be schedulable on a resource partition A is:
div.formula: |T | i=1 c i min(d i , p i ) -R(A) ≤ α(A) (1)
div.p: Theorem 1 is restricted in the sense that it requires all tasks' key parameters to be integers, which means their values must be integral multiples of the time-slice length. Such an assumption has its own demerits due to the following reasons. According to Definition 1, inside a time slice, no preemptions between VMs are allowed. However, within a time slice, different tasks in the same VM may preempt each other based on the task-level scheduling algorithms. Thus, the arrival time, WCET, and period can certainly be non-integral multiples of the time-slice length in practical cases. This means we need schedulability tests applicable for non-restricted tasks.

We present a task set as an example to illustrate why Theorem 1 only works for restricted task sets. The task set in Fig. 3 contains only one task and is deployed on a 2/7 resource partition. The WCET of the task is 0.3 while its deadline and period are both 3.1. Though such a task set satisfies Equation 1 because 0.3/(3.1-2) = 0.27 < 2/7, it is unschedulable when a job of the task arrives at time 3. This is because Theorem 1 only applies to tasks whose key parameters are integers.

Next, we present a new sufficient schedulability test. Note that this schedulability test not only accepts tasks whose key parameters are positive real numbers, it can also handle the task sets with both periodic and sporadic tasks. This brings about great convenience when applying the schedulability tests in industrial usage.

Compared to Theorem 1, Theorem 2 offers a schedulability test applicable to a task set where tasks' key parameters do not have any restrictions and a task can either be periodic or sporadic. This new schedulability test is more general and can be used more conveniently in practical industrial systems. Besides, Theorem 2 can also be used to calculate the minimum availability factor needed under different supply regularities when given the knowledge of the task set on a VM. This is beneficial when VM developers have to determine what resource partition the VM should require to offer real-time performance guarantees to the task set on the VM.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULING FOR INTRA-VM DEPENDENT TASKS
div.p: With more complicated applications deployed on virtualized systems, the intra-VM dependency exists between tasks on the same VM. The tasks with dependency can be modeled as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) [11,10,12,18]. For example, Fig. 4(a) shows a sample task system with interdependency between tasks. Specifically, each node could be a subjob of a task [18] or a job of a task [10] depending on the programming model. Each arrow represents a mandatory data transmission. For instance, N 5 pointing to N 4 means that the output of N 5 is the input of N 4 . Therefore, N 4 cannot start execution until N 5 is completed. Accordingly, a DAG, as shown in Fig. 4(b), can be generated. Task sets similar to the sample widely exist in complicated applications, which are deployed on virtualized systems more often nowadays [27]. Now, we formally defined a DAG N , which represents a set of inter-dependent tasks and is the input of task-level scheduling. In a DAG N , as shown in Fig. 4(b), each node N i has its corresponding arbitrary deadline D i , and its WCET c i . A node N i cannot be executed until all of its predecessors have been completed [11].

While using DAG to model tasks with dependency has already been studied, previous works [10,11,12,18] assume that the tasks are executed on one or more dedicated CPUs instead of a VM that only occupies a fraction of the CPU resource. The difference between a task scheduled on a dedicated CPU and that on a VM is: (1) on a dedicated CPU, it only takes 1 time slice of wall-clock time [20] to get 1 time slice of execution time for the task scheduled; (2) For a VM, it may take longer than 1 time slice of wall-clock time to get 1 time slice of execution time for the task scheduled. In short, the wall-clock time needed to execute C time slices on a VM that owns the resource partition A includes the waiting time when the CPU is allocated to other resource partitions and the execution time when the CPU is allocated to A. The wall-clock time needed is always larger than or equal to the execution time on a VM. To offer real-time performance guarantees, we need to know the longest wall-clock time needed such that C time slices of execution time are always guaranteed for a given resource partition A.

div.p: With the knowledge of the longest wall-clock time required to guarantee an execution time of C r on a VM, we further introduce a tuned approach to schedule intra-VM dependent tasks. This approach, as shown in Algorithm 1, is inspired from [10]. It computes the effective deadline Di based on the longest wall-clock time (ω i ) for each node N i and its original deadline D i . EDF then uses this newly computed Di as the priority of each node N i ∈ N .

Specifically, the effective deadline of N i , which is Di , is calculated as the minimum value among its original deadline D i and the successor's effective deadlines Dj minus that successor N j 's ω j , i.e., Di = min(D i , {D j -ω j :
div.formula: N i → N j }).
div.p: Here, N i → N j means N j is the successor of N i . Due to the calculation approaches of effective deadlines, the effective deadline of each node must be calculated in reversed topological order. Taking the DAG shown in Fig. 4 as an example. We must calculate the effective deadline of N 1 first. Since N 1 has no successor, D1 = D 1 . Then, we can calculate N 2 , N 4 and N 3 's effective deadlines. Specifically, D2 = min(D 2 , D1ω 1 ) and the same applies to N 3 and N 4 . After their effective deadlines are calculated, we can calculate that of N 5 and N 6 . Since N 5 have two successors, D5 = min(D 5 , D2ω 2 , D4ω 4 ).

Next, we prove the optimality of the approach. Lemma 2: When applying EDF based on effective deadlines, the schedulability of all nodes will not be affected. Besides, for any node N i and N j whose Di ≤ Dj , scheduling N i before N j will not violate the dependency between N i and N j .

Proof: First, we prove the schedulability of all nodes will not be affected when scheduling with EDF using effective deadlines. To establish this, we need to prove that if the system is unschedulable under effective deadlines, the system is also unschedulable under original deadlines and vice versa.

When the system is unschedulable under effective deadlines, there must exist a node N i whose effective deadline Di is not satisfied. If N i has no successor, Di = D i according to the calculation in Algorithm 1. If N i has at least one successor, e.g., N j , the worst-case completion time of this successor is no smaller than Di + w j > D j . Therefore, the system is always unschedulable under original deadlines whenever the system is unschedulable under effective deadlines.

When the system is unschedulable under original deadlines, it is also unschedulable under effective deadlines. This is because for any node N i , Di ≤ D i according to Algorithm 1. Thus, we prove the schedulability of all nodes will not be affected when using effective deadlines.

Next, we prove that scheduling any released node N i before N j with Di ≤ Dj will not violate the dependency between N i and N j . Assume the dependency between N i and N j is violated when scheduling N i before N j . This means N i is a direct or indirect successor of N j . According to Algorithm 1, Dj < Di since w i > 0. This contradicts the assumption and thus proves the claim.
Theorem 3: If a feasible schedule for the input of Algorithm 1 exists, Algorithm 1 will return a feasible schedule with no deadlines missed.

Proof: If a feasible schedule for the input of Algorithm 1 exists, we can always repeatedly switch nodes in the schedule so that the node with the earlier effective deadline is executed earlier. Such switching will not violate the dependency Fig. 5. A sample task that may suspends itself in a virtualized system. constraints according to Lemma 2. div.head: V. SCHEDULING INDEPENDENT SELF-SUSPENDED TASKS
div.p: In virtualized systems, it is common for tasks to selfsuspend when accessing external devices such as disks and sensors [14] or communicate with other partitions through Inter-Partition Communication (IPC) in some hypervisors, i.e., XtratuM [28,13]. Whenever a task attempts to read data from an external device or another partition, it will have to wait for the reply before it can continue the computation. Therefore, between different computation phases of a task, there exist self-suspension intervals. For example, the task shown in Fig. 5 is a typical sample existing in virtualized systems. This task needs to read the data from an external sensor after its first computation phase. The time between the request sent by the task and the reply received by the task results in a self-suspension period.

In some real-time systems, especially embedded systems, the time a job needs to self-suspend itself is known a priori. This is possible because all the I/O access to the external devices and IPC are actions performed by the code segments and
Fig. 6. An example task T 1 with c 1,1 = 1.5, c 1,2 = 0.5, s 1,1 = 2.5 and
div.formula: d i = p i = 10.
div.p: the code segments are all known a priori. Thus, the segmented (or multi-segment) self-suspension model is proposed [14,29].

For a task set T = {T 1 , T 2 , ..., T n }, each task T i is a sporadic task defined by (c i , d i , p i ) and a list of computation and suspension segments (c i,1 , s i,1 , c i,2 , s i,2 , ..., c i,mi+1 ). Here, c i is the total WCET of each job in T i where c i = mi j=1 c i,j and s i,1 , s i,2 , ..., s i,mi are the lengths of the suspension phases. In total, there are m i suspensions and m i + 1 computation phases. d i is the relative deadline of T i and p i is the minimum separation time. Without loss of generality, we assume d i ≤ p i .

We use an example in Fig. 6(a) to further illustrate this task model. In Fig. 6, we show a sample task set with only one task T 1 whose c 1 = 2, d 1 = p 1 = 10. Besides, c 1,1 = 1.5, c 1,2 = 0.5 and s 1,1 = 2.5. When executed, the first computation phase, which lasts 1.5 time slices, will be executed first. The suspension segment lasting another 1.5 time slices follows immediately. Next, the second computation phase will be executed. Similar execution behavior can be observed when the same task is executed in a VM with some differences. As shown in Fig. 6(b), the wall-clock time needed for executing each computation phase is actually longer than the WCET because some time slices are occupied by other VMs scheduled on the same CPU. The suspension segments, on the other hand, have the same length as that on a single CPU. The difference in the execution time of the computation phase makes it compulsory to develop a new schedulability test even though tasks are scheduled using the same scheduling approach on the VM as the one used on a single CPU.

The scheduling of self-suspended tasks is NP-hard and traditional scheduling algorithms, such as EDF, yield rather poor performance without consideration of relative deadlines for each computation phase [14]. Therefore, Fixed-Relative-Deadline (FRD) strategy is proposed to solve the scheduling problem of self-suspended tasks. The main idea of FRD is to treat each computation phase as a subjob and generate a relative deadline for each subjob. Then, subjobs are scheduled using EDF. Note that there is an implicit dependency between different subjobs from the same task, which implies a computation phase of a task will not be available for execution until all computation phases before being completed. There are multiple approaches to generate the relative deadline for each subjob, e.g., proportional relative deadline [30] and Equal- Deadline Assignment (EDA) [14,29]. These FRD approaches can also be used for task scheduling on a VM to generate relative deadlines for subjobs without any modifications. Utilizing the FRD approach, the scheduling of the task set and the schedulability test can both be polynomial. However, the available schedulability tests [14] are all established on dedicated CPUs instead of virtualized systems.

In this paper, we do not evaluate the performance, i.e., the speed-up factors [14], of different FRD approaches. Instead, we establish schedulability tests taking the task set scheduled by an FRD approach as an input. This means we assume the relative deadline of each subjob is known a priori. Specifically, d i,j represents the relative deadline for the jth subjob of task T i . div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper further explores the task-level scheduling problems based on the RRP model, which has not been solved in previous works. Specifically, this paper establishes schedulability tests on a single VM for task sets 1) whose tasks may contain key parameters which are not integral multiples of the time-slice length; 2) whose tasks have interdependency among them; 3) whose tasks may self-suspend themselves to wait for internal or external activities.

This paper is the first attempt to investigate the scheduling of different types of tasks on a VM based on the RRP model; many open problems still remain to be explored. For instance, the overhead brought by the schedulability tests proposed needs further theoretical and experimental evaluations. The performance of FRD algorithms in virtualized systems should be further evaluated in terms of the speedup factor. Also, while the RRP model has been implemented on Xen [31], practical experiments and case studies regarding task-level scheduling can also offer more insights on the performance of different scheduling algorithms on various types of tasks.
